title: What is NumPy?
NumPy: the absolute basics for beginners
text:
NumPy: the absolute basics for beginners
 Welcome to the absolute beginner’s guide to NumPy!
 
 NumPy (Numerical Python) is an open source Python library that’s widely used in science and engineering. The NumPy library contains multidimensional array data structures, such as the homogeneous, N-dimensional ndarray, and a large library of functions that operate efficiently on these data structures. Learn more about NumPy at What is NumPy, and if you have comments or suggestions, please reach out!
 
 How to import NumPy
 After installing NumPy, it may be imported into Python code like:
 
 import numpy as np
 This widespread convention allows access to NumPy features with a short, recognizable prefix (np.) while distinguishing NumPy features from others that have the same name.
 
 Reading the example code
 Throughout the NumPy documentation, you will find blocks that look like:
 
 a = np.array([[1, 2, 3],
  [4, 5, 6]])
 a.shape
 (2, 3)
 Text preceded by >>> or ... is input, the code that you would enter in a script or at a Python prompt. Everything else is output, the results of running your code. Note that >>> and ... are not part of the code and may cause an error if entered at a Python prompt.
 
 To run the code in the examples, you can copy and paste it into a Python script or REPL, or use the experimental interactive examples in the browser provided in various locations in the documentation.
 
 Why use NumPy?
 Python lists are excellent, general-purpose containers. They can be “heterogeneous”, meaning that they can contain elements of a variety of types, and they are quite fast when used to perform individual operations on a handful of elements.
 
 Depending on the characteristics of the data and the types of operations that need to be performed, other containers may be more appropriate; by exploiting these characteristics, we can improve speed, reduce memory consumption, and offer a high-level syntax for performing a variety of common processing tasks. NumPy shines when there are large quantities of “homogeneous” (same-type) data to be processed on the CPU.

title: Guide to NumPy
text: Object Essentials NumPy provides two fundamental objects: an N-dimensional array object (ndarray) and a universal function object (ufunc). In addition, there are other objects that build on top of these which you may find useful in your work, and these will be discussed later. The current chapter will provide background information on just the ndarray and the ufunc that will be important for understanding the attributes and methods to be discussed later. An N-dimensional array is a homogeneous collection of “items” indexed using N integers. There are two essential pieces of information that define an N-dimensional array: 1) the shape of the array, and 2) the kind of item the array is composed of. The shape of the array is a tuple of N integers (one for each dimension) that provides information on how far the index can vary along that dimension. The other important information describing an array is the kind of item the array is composed of. Because every ndarray is a homogeneous collection of exactly the same data-type, every item takes up the same size block of memory, and each block of memory in the array is interpreted in exactly the same way1 .

title: From Python to Numpy
text:
Title: NumPy Vectorization
 
 Vectorization is one of the fundamental concepts in NumPy and one of the main differences between NumPy programming and traditional Python programming. Instead of processing elements one at a time using explicit loops, vectorization performs operations on entire arrays simultaneously.
 
 Learning NumPy often requires changing the way problems are approached. Rather than writing loops that update one element after another, computations are expressed as operations on complete arrays. This programming style relies on arrays, views, and universal functions (ufuncs) to perform calculations efficiently.
 
 The primary advantage of vectorization is performance. Vectorized operations are implemented using optimized compiled code, allowing NumPy to execute numerical computations much faster than equivalent Python loops. This approach also reduces the amount of Python code required, resulting in shorter and often more expressive programs.
 
 Many algorithms can be reformulated from an iterative process into a sequence of array operations. Instead of computing each intermediate value individually, the complete dataset is generated or transformed first, and then NumPy applies optimized operations to the entire array. This eliminates much of the overhead associated with Python loops and takes advantage of highly optimized numerical libraries.
 
 Although vectorization significantly improves performance, it can also reduce code readability when complex array operations are combined into a single expression. Highly optimized vectorized code may be more difficult to understand than a straightforward implementation using loops. For this reason, clear variable names, comments, and well-structured code are important to maintain readability while preserving the performance benefits of NumPy.
 
 Vectorization is the foundation of efficient numerical computing with NumPy and is one of the key concepts required to write high-performance scientific and data analysis applications.

title: NumPy quickstart
text:
The basics
 NumPy’s main object is the homogeneous multidimensional array. It is a table of elements (usually numbers), all of the same type, indexed by a tuple of non-negative integers. In NumPy dimensions are called axes.
 For example, the array for the coordinates of a point in 3D space, [1, 2, 1], has one axis. That axis has 3 elements in it, so we say it has a length of 3. In the example pictured below, the array has 2 axes. The first axis has a length of 2, the second axis has a length of 3.
 [[1., 0., 0.],
  [0., 1., 2.]]
 NumPy’s array class is called ndarray. It is also known by the alias array. Note that numpy.array is not the same as the Standard Python Library class array.array, which only handles one-dimensional arrays and offers less functionality. The more important attributes of an ndarray object are:
 ndarray.ndim
 the number of axes (dimensions) of the array.
 ndarray.shape
 the dimensions of the array. This is a tuple of integers indicating the size of the array in each dimension. For a matrix with n rows and m columns, shape will be (n,m). The length of the shape tuple is therefore the number of axes, ndim.
 ndarray.size
 the total number of elements of the array. This is equal to the product of the elements of shape.
 ndarray.dtype
 an object describing the type of the elements in the array. One can create or specify dtype’s using standard Python types. Additionally NumPy provides types of its own. numpy.int32, numpy.int16, and numpy.float64 are some examples.
 ndarray.itemsize
 the size in bytes of each element of the array. For example, an array of elements of type float64 has itemsize 8 (=64/8), while one of type complex32 has itemsize 4 (=32/8). It is equivalent to ndarray.dtype.itemsize.
 ndarray.data
 the buffer containing the actual elements of the array. Normally, we won’t need to use this attribute because we will access the elements in an array using indexing facilities.

title: Numpy tutorial
text:
NumPy is the fundamental package for scientific computing in Python. It provides a powerful N-dimensional array object (ndarray), efficient mathematical operations, broadcasting capabilities, tools for integrating C, C++, and Fortran code, and libraries for linear algebra, Fourier transforms, and random number generation.
 
 Although NumPy is primarily designed for scientific computing, it also serves as an efficient multidimensional container for general-purpose data. Its flexible data types and optimized memory representation make it suitable for numerical analysis, simulations, data processing, machine learning, and many other applications.
 
 Throughout this guide, the Game of Life is used as a practical example to demonstrate how NumPy arrays and vectorized operations can simplify algorithms that would otherwise require nested Python loops.
 
NumPy Array Creation
 
 NumPy arrays are created using the numpy.array() function. When an array is created, NumPy automatically infers an appropriate data type unless one is explicitly specified.
 
 Every array has a shape that describes its dimensions and a dtype that specifies the type of data stored in each element. These properties can be inspected through the shape and dtype attributes.
 
 Elements of an array are accessed using row and column indices, while portions of an array can be extracted using slice notation.
 Title: NumPy Views and Slicing
 
 Slicing a NumPy array usually creates a view rather than a copy. A view shares the same underlying memory as the original array, so modifying the view also modifies the original array.
 
 This behavior differs from many Python objects and is one of the reasons NumPy can manipulate large datasets efficiently without unnecessary memory allocation.
 
 If an independent copy is required, it must be created explicitly.

text:
Creating NumPy Arrays
 
 NumPy provides several ways to create arrays depending on the type of data required.
 
 Arrays can be initialized from Python lists, including nested lists for multidimensional arrays. NumPy also provides specialized creation functions for common cases, such as creating arrays filled with zeros, arrays filled with ones, constant-value arrays, identity matrices, and arrays containing random values.
 
 These creation functions allow developers to quickly allocate arrays with a desired shape and initial values without manually specifying every element.
 
 Common array creation functions include:
 
 - zeros: creates an array where all elements are zero.
 - ones: creates an array where all elements are one.
 - full: creates an array filled with a specified value.
 - eye: creates an identity matrix.
 - random functions: create arrays containing random values.
 
 Title: NumPy Array Indexing and Slicing
 
 NumPy provides several methods for accessing elements and subarrays. Similar to Python lists, arrays can be sliced to extract portions of the data.
 
 Because NumPy arrays can have multiple dimensions, slicing must specify the range for each dimension. A slice selects a portion of an array while preserving the relationship with the original data.
 
 A key characteristic of NumPy slicing is that it returns a view instead of a copy. A view shares the same underlying memory as the original array, meaning that changes made to the sliced array can also modify the original array.
 
 When combining integer indexing with slice indexing, NumPy may reduce the number of dimensions of the resulting array. Using only slices preserves the original number of dimensions.

title: An introduction to Numpy and Scipy
text:
Importing NumPy and ndarray Basics
 
 NumPy is the core library for scientific computing in Python. It provides a high-performance multidimensional array object called ndarray and a collection of tools for efficient numerical operations.
 
 The standard way to import NumPy is using the alias np. This convention allows access to NumPy functions and objects using a shorter prefix while keeping the origin of functions clear.
 
 The central feature of NumPy is the ndarray object. Unlike Python lists, NumPy arrays store elements of a single data type, usually numerical values such as integers or floating-point numbers. This homogeneous structure allows NumPy to perform operations on large amounts of data efficiently.
 
 NumPy arrays can be one-dimensional or multidimensional. A multidimensional array is organized using axes, where each axis represents a dimension of the data. The shape attribute describes the size of each dimension, while dtype describes the type of values stored in the array.
 Title: Creating NumPy Arrays
 
 NumPy provides several methods for creating arrays. Arrays can be initialized from Python lists or generated using specialized functions.
 
 The array function converts Python sequences into NumPy ndarray objects. Nested lists can be used to create multidimensional arrays.
 
 NumPy also provides functions for creating arrays with predefined values:
 
 - zeros creates arrays filled with zeros.
 - ones creates arrays filled with ones.
 - full creates arrays where every element has the same specified value.
 - identity creates identity matrices.
 - random functions generate arrays containing random values.
 
 These creation methods allow efficient allocation of numerical data structures with a specific shape and initial state.
 Title: NumPy Array Indexing and Slicing
 
 NumPy arrays support indexing and slicing operations similar to Python lists, but they extend these concepts to multiple dimensions.
 
 Elements in multidimensional arrays are accessed by providing an index for each axis. Slicing allows extracting portions of an array by specifying ranges along each dimension.
 
 A slice of a NumPy array usually returns a view instead of a copy. A view shares the same underlying memory as the original array, meaning that modifications made to the sliced array can affect the original array.
 
 When using integer indexing together with slicing, NumPy may reduce the number of dimensions of the resulting array. Using only slices preserves the dimensional structure of the original array.

title: FastAPI
text:
FastAPI es un framework moderno de Python utilizado para crear APIs web de alto rendimiento. Está diseñado alrededor de los type hints estándar de Python y permite construir servicios HTTP con validación automática de datos, documentación interactiva y una sintaxis sencilla.
 
 FastAPI combina dos tecnologías principales: Starlette, utilizada para las funcionalidades web y manejo de solicitudes HTTP, y Pydantic, encargado de la validación y serialización de datos mediante modelos basados en tipos de Python.
 
 Una de las características principales de FastAPI es su alto rendimiento. Gracias a su arquitectura basada en ASGI y al uso eficiente de operaciones asíncronas, puede alcanzar velocidades comparables a frameworks desarrollados en otros lenguajes como Node.js o Go.
 
 FastAPI reduce la cantidad de código necesario para desarrollar APIs porque utiliza las anotaciones de tipo de Python para generar validaciones automáticas. Por ejemplo, si un parámetro está definido como entero, FastAPI puede validar automáticamente que la entrada recibida tenga el formato correcto.
 
 Además, genera documentación interactiva automáticamente utilizando los estándares OpenAPI y JSON Schema. Esto permite disponer de interfaces como Swagger UI y ReDoc sin necesidad de escribir documentación manual.
 
 Las principales ventajas de FastAPI son:
 - Desarrollo rápido gracias a la reducción de código repetitivo.
 - Validación automática de datos.
 - Compatibilidad con programación síncrona y asíncrona.
 - Generación automática de documentación.
 - Integración sencilla con sistemas de producción.
 
 FastAPI es utilizado frecuentemente para construir APIs REST, microservicios, servicios de machine learning y aplicaciones backend modernas en Python.
 FastAPI está construido sobre dos componentes principales: Starlette y Pydantic.
 
 Starlette proporciona la capa web del framework. Se encarga del manejo de rutas, solicitudes HTTP, respuestas, middleware, sesiones y soporte para aplicaciones ASGI.
 
 Pydantic proporciona la validación y transformación de datos. Permite definir modelos utilizando clases Python con anotaciones de tipos. Cuando una API recibe información externa, Pydantic verifica automáticamente que los datos cumplan con la estructura esperada.
 
 La combinación de ambos componentes permite que FastAPI pueda recibir datos, validarlos, procesarlos y devolver respuestas estructuradas con poco código.
 
 El flujo típico de una solicitud en FastAPI es:
 
 1. Un cliente envía una solicitud HTTP.
 2. FastAPI identifica la ruta correspondiente.
 3. Los parámetros recibidos son validados utilizando los tipos definidos.
 4. Pydantic convierte los datos al formato esperado.
 5. La función asociada a la ruta procesa la información.

title: Developing Your First Spring Boot Application
text:
Spring Boot es un framework basado en Java diseñado para simplificar la creación y despliegue de aplicaciones empresariales, especialmente aplicaciones web y APIs.
 
 Spring Boot forma parte del ecosistema Spring y proporciona una configuración automática que reduce la cantidad de código necesario para iniciar una aplicación. En lugar de configurar manualmente servidores, dependencias y componentes internos, Spring Boot utiliza convenciones y valores predeterminados para crear aplicaciones listas para ejecutarse.
 
 Una de sus principales características es el uso de starters, que son conjuntos de dependencias agrupadas para casos de uso específicos. Por ejemplo, una aplicación web puede utilizar un starter que incluya automáticamente las bibliotecas necesarias para crear controladores HTTP, manejar solicitudes web y ejecutar un servidor embebido.
 
 Spring Boot permite desarrollar aplicaciones utilizando herramientas comunes del ecosistema Java como Maven o Gradle. Ambos sistemas gestionan la construcción del proyecto, las dependencias y las tareas de compilación.
 
 Las características principales de Spring Boot incluyen:
 
 - Configuración automática de componentes.
 - Servidores embebidos como Tomcat.
 - Gestión simplificada de dependencias mediante starters.
 - Integración con el ecosistema Spring.
 - Facilidad para crear APIs REST y aplicaciones web.
 - Preparación para despliegues en entornos de producción.
 
 Spring Boot es ampliamente utilizado para desarrollar microservicios, aplicaciones empresariales y servicios backend debido a su productividad y facilidad de mantenimiento.

 Los starters de Spring Boot son conjuntos de dependencias preconfiguradas que simplifican la creación de aplicaciones.
 
 En un proyecto Java tradicional, el desarrollador debe seleccionar manualmente cada biblioteca necesaria y configurar sus versiones. Spring Boot reduce este trabajo proporcionando starters que agrupan dependencias relacionadas.
 
 Por ejemplo, para desarrollar una aplicación web se utiliza normalmente un starter web. Este starter incluye componentes necesarios como:
 
 - Framework Spring MVC.
 - Manejo de solicitudes HTTP.
 - Serialización de datos.
 - Servidor web embebido.
 
 Los starters también ayudan a mantener versiones compatibles entre las diferentes bibliotecas. Spring Boot utiliza un sistema de gestión de dependencias que permite omitir versiones individuales porque el framework define versiones recomendadas y compatibles.
 
 Cuando se agrega un starter a un proyecto, las herramientas de construcción como Maven o Gradle descargan automáticamente las dependencias necesarias y sus dependencias transitivas.

title: Python Types Intro
text: Python supports optional type hints (also called type annotations), which allow declaring the type of variables, function parameters and return values. Declaring types enables editors and tools to provide better support, including autocompletion, type checking and error detection. FastAPI is based on these type hints and uses them as the foundation for many of its features. Type hints can be declared for standard Python types such as str, int, float, bool and bytes. The typing module provides additional types such as Any for values that can have any type. Python also supports generic types, allowing collections to specify the type of their elements, for example list[str], tuple[int, int, str], set[bytes] and dict[str, float]. Union types can be declared using the | operator, such as int | str, and optional values can be represented with str | None. Classes can also be used as types to indicate that a variable or parameter must be an instance of a specific class. FastAPI uses Pydantic models to define the structure of data through classes with typed attributes. Pydantic validates input data, converts values to the required types when possible and returns typed objects. Python also provides Annotated, which allows attaching metadata to type hints while preserving the original type. FastAPI uses this metadata to define the behavior of parameters and other application components. FastAPI uses type hints to define requirements for path parameters, query parameters, headers, request bodies and dependencies, convert request data to the declared types, validate incoming data, automatically generate validation errors and produce OpenAPI documentation with interactive API documentation.

title: Primeros pasos
text:
FastAPI es un framework web de Python utilizado para construir APIs. Una aplicación básica se crea importando la clase FastAPI y creando una instancia de la aplicación mediante app = FastAPI(). Esta instancia es el punto principal de interacción para definir rutas, operaciones HTTP y comportamiento de la API. FastAPI es una clase que hereda directamente de Starlette, por lo que también permite utilizar funcionalidades proporcionadas por ese framework web. Una aplicación mínima puede definir una ruta utilizando un decorador como @app.get("/"), donde el decorador indica que la función asociada manejará solicitudes HTTP GET para el path /. La función debajo del decorador es conocida como una path operation function y será ejecutada cuando FastAPI reciba una solicitud que coincida con la ruta y el método HTTP configurado.
 
 Para ejecutar una aplicación FastAPI se utiliza el comando fastapi dev, que inicia un servidor de desarrollo utilizando Uvicorn y expone la aplicación normalmente en http://127.0.0.1:8000. Al acceder a la URL configurada, la aplicación devuelve la respuesta definida por la función, como un objeto JSON. Las funciones de rutas pueden definirse utilizando async def para programación asíncrona o como funciones normales con def. FastAPI permite retornar diferentes tipos de datos, como diccionarios, listas, valores simples como str e int, además de modelos de Pydantic y otros objetos que pueden convertirse automáticamente a JSON.
 
 En FastAPI, un path representa la parte de la URL utilizada para identificar un recurso o endpoint, mientras que una operation representa un método HTTP utilizado para comunicarse con ese path. Los métodos HTTP más utilizados son GET para obtener datos, POST para crear información, PUT para actualizar datos y DELETE para eliminar recursos. También existen otros métodos como PATCH, OPTIONS, HEAD y TRACE. Los decoradores de operaciones permiten asociar funciones Python con estos métodos, por ejemplo @app.get(), @app.post(), @app.put() y @app.delete(). Esta estructura permite construir APIs organizadas donde cada ruta tiene una función específica encargada de procesar las solicitudes y devolver respuestas.

title: Concurrency and async / await
text:
FastAPI supports asynchronous programming using Python's async def and await syntax to improve performance in web applications. Asynchronous code allows a program to handle waiting operations efficiently by pausing a task when it needs to wait for an external operation and continuing with other tasks in the meantime.
 
 In FastAPI, path operation functions can be declared with async def when they use third-party libraries that support await. For example, when a library requires calling an asynchronous operation like results = await some_library(), the path operation function must also be asynchronous. The await keyword tells Python to wait for the operation to complete while allowing the application to perform other work during that waiting period.
 
 If a third-party library does not support await, such as many database libraries, path operation functions can be declared normally using def. FastAPI allows mixing def and async def path operation functions depending on the requirements of each operation. When using normal def functions, FastAPI runs them in an external threadpool to prevent blocking the server.
 
 Asynchronous programming is mainly useful for I/O bound operations, where most of the execution time is spent waiting for external resources. Examples include receiving data from clients through the network, sending responses, reading files, writing files, calling remote APIs, and waiting for database queries to return results.
 
 Concurrency and parallelism are related but different concepts. Concurrency allows multiple tasks to make progress while some of them are waiting, while parallelism means executing multiple tasks at the same time using multiple processors. FastAPI takes advantage of concurrency for web applications and can also benefit from parallelism and multiprocessing for CPU bound workloads such as image processing, computer vision, machine learning, and deep learning applications.
 
 Python asynchronous programming uses coroutines, which are functions created with async def that can be paused when reaching an await expression and resumed later when the awaited operation finishes. This asynchronous model is one of the reasons FastAPI achieves high performance, as it allows efficient handling of multiple requests.
 
 FastAPI is built on top of Starlette and uses this asynchronous foundation to provide high performance for modern web APIs. Developers should use async def when working with asynchronous libraries and def when using blocking libraries, allowing FastAPI to apply the appropriate execution model for each case.

title: FastAPI CLI
text:
FastAPI CLI is a command line program used to serve FastAPI applications, manage FastAPI projects, and run applications in different environments. When FastAPI is added to a project, for example with uv add "fastapi[standard]", it includes the CLI tool that can be executed from the terminal.
 
 For development purposes, FastAPI applications can be started using the fastapi dev command. This command automatically detects the FastAPI application, starts the development server, and provides access to the API and its documentation. By default, fastapi dev enables auto-reload, which automatically restarts the server when code changes are detected. This feature is useful during development but is resource-intensive and should not be used in production environments.
 
 Internally, FastAPI CLI uses Uvicorn, a high-performance ASGI server used to run FastAPI applications. The CLI automatically searches for the FastAPI app object, commonly expecting an object named app inside a file such as main.py. For example, it can import the application using from main import app.
 
 The application entrypoint can be configured explicitly using the pyproject.toml file. By defining the entrypoint property, FastAPI CLI knows exactly where the application instance is located. For example, entrypoint = "main:app" indicates that the FastAPI instance should be imported from the main.py module. This approach is recommended because other tools, such as VS Code extensions or FastAPI Cloud, can also detect the application correctly.
 
 The fastapi run command starts FastAPI in production mode. Unlike fastapi dev, it disables auto-reload by default and listens on 0.0.0.0, allowing access from external clients that can communicate with the machine. This configuration is commonly used when deploying applications in production environments, including containers.
 
 The main difference between fastapi dev and fastapi run is their intended use. fastapi dev is designed for local development with automatic reload and localhost access, while fastapi run is designed for production execution with a stable server configuration.
 
 FastAPI CLI also manages environment behavior. When running fastapi dev, the FASTAPI_ENV environment variable is set to development if it is not already defined. This allows applications to adjust their startup behavior depending on the environment. The conventional values are development and production. For production deployments, applications should explicitly configure the required environment settings.

title: FastAPI features
text:
FastAPI is a modern Python framework designed around open standards and standard Python type declarations. It uses OpenAPI for API creation, including path operations, parameters, request bodies, and security definitions. It also uses JSON Schema to automatically document data models, allowing automatic client code generation in multiple programming languages.
 
 One of the main features of FastAPI is its automatic API documentation. Because it is based on OpenAPI, it provides interactive documentation interfaces by default, including Swagger UI and ReDoc. Swagger UI allows developers to explore, call, and test API endpoints directly from the browser, while ReDoc provides an alternative documentation interface.
 
 FastAPI is built around modern Python type hints, using standard Python syntax without requiring a new framework-specific language. Through Pydantic, developers can define data structures using Python classes and type annotations. These definitions provide editor support, automatic validation, and better developer experience.
 
 The framework was designed to provide strong editor integration, including autocomplete and type checking. FastAPI improves productivity by allowing developers to discover available attributes, detect incorrect values, and work with complex request bodies without constantly checking documentation.
 
 FastAPI includes automatic validation for many Python data types, such as dictionaries, lists, strings, integers, and floats. It also supports validation for more specialized types including URLs, emails, and UUIDs. This validation is handled by Pydantic, which provides robust data parsing and validation capabilities.
 
 Security and authentication are integrated using OpenAPI security schemes and Starlette features. FastAPI supports HTTP Basic authentication, OAuth2 with JWT tokens, API keys through headers, query parameters, and cookies. These security tools are designed to integrate easily with databases, data stores, and existing systems.
 
 FastAPI provides a powerful Dependency Injection system that allows dependencies to be reused throughout applications. Dependencies can contain their own dependencies, creating a hierarchy automatically managed by the framework. This system supports authentication, database connections, request validation, and other reusable application components.
 
 FastAPI is fully compatible with Starlette and inherits its features, including high performance, WebSocket support, background tasks, startup and shutdown events, HTTPX test client, CORS, GZip, static files, streaming responses, sessions, and cookies.
 
 FastAPI is also fully compatible with Pydantic features, allowing developers to validate complex nested data structures, create custom data types, and use validated models throughout their applications. Its design provides automatic validation, documentation, editor support, and production-ready API development using standard Python.

title: FastAPI
text:
FastAPI is a modern, fast (high-performance), web framework for building APIs with Python based on standard Python type hints. It is designed to create APIs quickly while maintaining high performance, simple code, automatic documentation, and production-ready features.
 
 The key features of FastAPI include being fast, fast to code, intuitive, easy to learn, short, robust, and standards-based. It provides very high performance, comparable to NodeJS and Go, thanks to Starlette and Pydantic. It is one of the fastest Python frameworks available.
 
 FastAPI is based on open standards. It uses OpenAPI for API creation, including declarations of path operations, parameters, request bodies, security, and other API components. It also uses JSON Schema for automatic data model documentation. Because FastAPI follows these standards, it can support automatic client code generation for many programming languages.
 
 FastAPI is built on top of Starlette and Pydantic. Starlette provides the web functionality, while Pydantic manages data handling and validation. Because FastAPI is fully compatible with Starlette, developers can use features such as WebSockets, background tasks, startup and shutdown events, CORS, GZip, Static Files, Streaming responses, and session support.
 
 Pydantic allows developers to use standard Python type declarations instead of learning a new syntax or schema language. By defining models with Python classes and type hints, FastAPI can automatically validate incoming data, convert data types, generate JSON Schema documentation, and provide better editor support.
 
 This combination of FastAPI, Starlette, and Pydantic creates a framework focused on performance, developer productivity, automatic validation, and modern API development practices.

title: fast-api-learn
text:
FastAPI is a modern Python web framework focused on building APIs with high performance, simplicity, and production readiness. It is considered one of the fastest modern Python frameworks because it supports asynchronous programming (async) and Python type hints, which improve performance, validation, and developer experience.
 
 FastAPI is designed to be easy to learn, fast to code, and ready for production applications. It is commonly used for creating REST APIs because it provides automatic documentation, strong type support, and modern features from Python. The framework uses technologies such as Starlette for web functionality and Pydantic for data validation.
 
 To install FastAPI, you can use pip:
 
 pip3 install fastapi[all]
 
 FastAPI applications need a server to run. A common choice is Uvicorn, an ASGI server designed for high-performance Python applications.
 
 Install Uvicorn:
 
 pip3 install uvicorn[standard]
 
 To create your first FastAPI API, create a project folder called app. Inside this folder, create a file called main.py.
 
 The first step is importing FastAPI and creating an application instance:
 
 from fastapi import FastAPI
 
 app = FastAPI()
 
 The variable app represents the FastAPI application. It will be the main object used to define routes, endpoints, and application behavior.
 
 A route can be created using decorators. For example:
 
 @app.get("/")
 def index():
  return "HELLO WORLD"
 
 The decorator @app.get("/") defines an HTTP GET endpoint. When a client sends a GET request to the root path /, FastAPI executes the index() function and returns the response.
 
 To start the development server, run:
 
 uvicorn main:app --reload
 
 The command works by importing the FastAPI instance from the file:
 
 main:app
 
 where:
 
 main is the Python file.
 app is the FastAPI instance created with FastAPI().
 
 The --reload option enables automatic server restarting whenever code changes are detected. This option is useful during development because you do not need to manually restart the server after modifying your code.
 
 With only a few lines of code, FastAPI provides a working API endpoint ready to receive HTTP requests.

title: Advanced FastAPI Features with Python Roadmap
text:
The Advanced FastAPI Features with Python Roadmap is designed to deepen FastAPI knowledge by exploring advanced concepts used in real-world backend development. The goal is to learn how to build secure, scalable, optimized APIs and prepare for backend and AI/ML engineering interviews.
 
 FastAPI provides powerful features that go beyond creating simple API endpoints. Advanced development requires understanding authentication, authorization, middleware, asynchronous programming, and performance monitoring. These features allow developers to create applications that are secure, efficient, and capable of handling large numbers of requests.
 
 One of the main topics is Authentication and Authorization. Authentication focuses on verifying the identity of users, while authorization determines what actions users are allowed to perform. FastAPI commonly uses JWT (JSON Web Token) based authentication to protect API endpoints. With JWT, applications can securely manage user sessions and restrict access to protected resources.
 
 Another important area is Middleware and Async Programming. Middleware allows developers to process requests and responses globally before they reach the endpoint. It can be used for tasks such as logging, security checks, request timing, and modifying responses.
 
 Async programming with async and await improves API scalability by allowing non-blocking operations. This is especially useful when APIs communicate with databases, external services, or other resources that require waiting time. Instead of blocking execution, FastAPI can handle multiple concurrent requests efficiently.
 
 The roadmap also covers Performance Metrics Visualization. Measuring API performance helps developers understand how their applications behave under different workloads. Important metrics include latency, which measures response time, and throughput, which measures how many requests an API can process.
 
 Mastering these advanced FastAPI features helps developers create production-ready applications. Security improvements come from JWT authentication and protected endpoints. Scalability improves through asynchronous programming and concurrency. Optimization becomes easier by analyzing performance metrics.
 
 These concepts are also highly relevant for backend developer and AI/ML engineer interviews because companies commonly evaluate knowledge of API security, performance, and scalable architecture.

title: Structuring Your Code
text:
Spring Boot does not force a specific project structure. Applications can be organized in different ways.
 However, following good package organization practices improves:
 • Maintainability. 
 • Component scanning. 
 • Project scalability. 
 • Team collaboration. 
 For applications organized by business domains, Spring recommends considering:
 Spring Modulith
 which helps create modular Spring Boot applications.
 Avoid Using the Default Package
 In Java, when a class has no package declaration, it belongs to the default package.
 Example:
 public class MyApplication {
 
 }
 without:
 package com.example.project;
 is considered a default package class.
 Spring Boot discourages this because it can create problems with:
 • @ComponentScan 
 • @ConfigurationPropertiesScan 
 • @EntityScan 
 • @SpringBootApplication 
 Reason:
 Spring may scan every class from every dependency JAR, creating unnecessary scanning and possible conflicts.
 Recommended Package Naming
 Spring Boot follows Java package conventions.
 Recommended format:
 reverse domain name
 Example:
 com.example.project
 Real company example:
 com.google.application
 Benefits:
 • Unique namespace. 
 • Avoids conflicts. 
 • Better organization. 
 Main Application Class Location
 The main Spring Boot class should normally be placed in the root package.
 Example:
 com
  └── example
  └── myapplication
  └── MyApplication.java
 The reason:
 The class containing:
 @SpringBootApplication
 defines the base package where Spring searches for components.
 Spring uses this location for:
 • Component scanning. 
 • Entity discovery. 
 • Configuration detection. 
 @SpringBootApplication Role
 The annotation:
 @SpringBootApplication
 combines three important annotations:
 @SpringBootConfiguration
 @EnableAutoConfiguration
 @ComponentScan
 It automatically enables:
 Component Scanning
 Searches classes annotated with:
 @Component
 @Service
 @Repository
 @Controller
 Auto Configuration
 Automatically configures Spring Boot based on dependencies.
 Example:
 Adding:
 spring-boot-starter-webmvc
 allows Spring Boot to configure:
 • Spring MVC. 
 • Embedded Tomcat. 
 • Web application settings. 
 Entity Scanning
 For JPA applications, Spring searches for:
 @Entity
 classes inside the main package and subpackages.
 Recommended Project Layout
 Example:
 com
  └── example
  └── myapplication
  |
  ├── MyApplication.java
  |
  ├── customer
  | ├── Customer.java
  | ├── CustomerController.java
  | ├── CustomerService.java
  | └── CustomerRepository.java
  |
  └── order
  ├── Order.java
  ├── OrderController.java
  ├── OrderService.java
  └── OrderRepository.java
 This structure organizes code by business domain.
 Example:
 Customer Domain
 Entity:
 Customer.java
 Handles database model.
 Controller:
 CustomerController.java
 Handles HTTP requests.
 Service:
 CustomerService.java
 Contains business logic.
 Repository:
 CustomerRepository.java
 Handles database communication.
 Main Application Class Example
 MyApplication.java
 package com.example.myapplication;
 
 import org.springframework.boot.SpringApplication;
 import org.springframework.boot.autoconfigure.SpringBootApplication;
 
 @SpringBootApplication
 public class MyApplication {
 
  public static void main(String[] args) {
 
  SpringApplication.run(
  MyApplication.class,
  args
  );
 
  }
 
 }
 The main() method starts the Spring Boot application.
 Concept Summary
 A good Spring Boot structure:
 • Avoids the default package. 
 • Uses reverse domain package naming. 
 • Places the main class in the root package. 
 • Uses domain-based organization. 
 • Allows Spring scanning to work correctly. 
 Example:
 root package
  |
  ├── customer
  |
  ├── order
  |
  └── MyApplication.java

title: SpringApplication
text:
SpringApplication is the main class used by Spring Boot to bootstrap and start an application from a main() method. It provides a simple way to initialize the Spring environment by creating the ApplicationContext, loading and configuring beans, applying application properties, and starting the embedded web server when required. In most applications, the startup process is handled by calling SpringApplication.run(MyApplication.class, args), which automatically performs the necessary configuration and initialization steps.
 
 When a Spring Boot application starts, it displays startup information such as the Spring Boot version, Java version, process ID, active profile, embedded server configuration, and total startup time. By default, these messages are displayed using the INFO logging level. Startup information can be disabled by setting spring.main.log-startup-info=false. Developers can also add custom startup information by overriding the logStartupInfo(boolean) method in a custom SpringApplication implementation.
 
 If an application fails during startup, Spring Boot uses FailureAnalyzer components to provide a clearer explanation of the problem and possible solutions. Instead of only showing a technical exception, Spring Boot can identify common issues, such as a port already being used, and suggest corrective actions. If the problem cannot be analyzed automatically, developers can enable debug mode with the --debug option to display the complete condition evaluation report and understand why the application could not start.
 
 SpringApplication supports lazy initialization, which allows beans to be created only when they are required instead of during application startup. This can improve startup time, especially in large applications with many beans. However, lazy initialization can delay the discovery of configuration errors because problems appear only when a specific bean is accessed. For this reason, lazy initialization is disabled by default and should be enabled carefully using the property spring.main.lazy-initialization=true.
 
 The default Spring Boot startup banner can be customized by adding a banner.txt file to the application classpath or by configuring the spring.banner.location property. The banner can display dynamic information such as the application version, Spring Boot version, and application title. It can also be disabled or modified programmatically using SpringApplication configuration methods.
 
 SpringApplication can be customized by creating a SpringApplication instance instead of using the static run() method. This allows developers to change default behaviors, configure startup options, and control how the application is initialized. For more advanced scenarios, SpringApplicationBuilder can be used to create multiple ApplicationContexts with parent-child relationships and provide a fluent configuration style.
 
 Spring Boot also manages application availability through Liveness and Readiness states. Liveness indicates whether the application is running correctly and can recover internally. If the liveness state fails, infrastructure platforms such as Kubernetes can restart the application. Readiness indicates whether the application is ready to receive traffic. These states are commonly exposed through Spring Boot Actuator health endpoints and Kubernetes probes.
 
 During the startup lifecycle, SpringApplication publishes different application events, including ApplicationStartingEvent, ApplicationStartedEvent, ApplicationReadyEvent, and ApplicationFailedEvent. These events allow components to execute logic at specific moments during application initialization. After startup, ApplicationRunner and CommandLineRunner can be used to execute tasks that must run before the application begins accepting requests. Finally, SpringApplication registers a JVM shutdown hook to close the ApplicationContext gracefully, and custom exit codes can be defined through the ExitCodeGenerator interface.

title: Running Your Application
text:
One of the biggest advantages of packaging your application as a jar and using an embedded HTTP server is that you can run your application as you would any other. The same applies to debugging Spring Boot applications. You do not need any special IDE plugins or extensions.
 
 The options below are best suited for running an application locally for development. For production deployment, see Packaging Your Application for Production.
 This section only covers jar-based packaging. If you choose to package your application as a war file, see your server and IDE documentation.
 Running From an IDE
 You can run a Spring Boot application from your IDE as a Java application. However, you first need to import your project. Import steps vary depending on your IDE and build system. Most IDEs can import Maven projects directly. For example, Eclipse users can select Import…​ → Existing Maven Projects from the File menu.
 
 If you cannot directly import your project into your IDE, you may be able to generate IDE metadata by using a build plugin. Maven includes plugins for Eclipse and IntelliJ IDEA. Gradle offers plugins for various IDEs.
 
 If you accidentally run a web application twice, you see a “Port already in use” error. Spring Tools users can use the Relaunch button rather than the Run button to ensure that any existing instance is closed.
 Running as a Packaged Application
 If you use the Spring Boot Maven or Gradle plugins to create an executable jar, you can run your application using java -jar, as shown in the following example:
 
 $ java -jar target/myapplication-0.0.1-SNAPSHOT.jar
 It is also possible to run a packaged application with remote debugging support enabled. Doing so lets you attach a debugger to your packaged application, as shown in the following example:
 
 $ java -agentlib:jdwp=server=y,transport=dt_socket,address=8000,suspend=n \
  -jar target/myapplication-0.0.1-SNAPSHOT.jar
 Using the Maven Plugin
 The Spring Boot Maven plugin includes a run goal that can be used to quickly compile and run your application. Applications run in an exploded form, as they do in your IDE. The following example shows a typical Maven command to run a Spring Boot application:
 
 $ mvn spring-boot:run
 You might also want to use the MAVEN_OPTS operating system environment variable, as shown in the following example:
 
 $ export MAVEN_OPTS=-Xmx1024m
 Using the Gradle Plugin
 The Spring Boot Gradle plugin also includes a bootRun task that can be used to run your application in an exploded form. The bootRun task is added whenever you apply the org.springframework.boot and java plugins and is shown in the following example:
 
 $ gradle bootRun
 You might also want to use the JAVA_OPTS operating system environment variable, as shown in the following example:
 
 $ export JAVA_OPTS=-Xmx1024m
 Hot Swapping
 Since Spring Boot applications are plain Java applications, JVM hot-swapping should work out of the box. JVM hot swapping is somewhat limited with the bytecode that it can replace. For a more complete solution, JRebel can be used.
 
 The spring-boot-devtools module also includes support for quick application restarts. See the Hot Swapping section in “How-to Guides” for details.

title: Installing Spring Boot
text:
Spring Boot can be used with “classic” Java development tools or installed as a command line tool. Either way, you need Java SDK v17 or higher. Before you begin, you should check your current Java installation by using the following command:
 
 $ java -version
 If you are new to Java development or if you want to experiment with Spring Boot, you might want to try the Spring Boot CLI (Command Line Interface) first. Otherwise, read on for “classic” installation instructions.
 
 Installation Instructions for the Java Developer
 You can use Spring Boot in the same way as any standard Java library. To do so, include the appropriate spring-boot-*.jar files on your classpath. Spring Boot does not require any special tools integration, so you can use any IDE or text editor. Also, there is nothing special about a Spring Boot application, so you can run and debug a Spring Boot application as you would any other Java program.
 
 Although you could copy Spring Boot jars, we generally recommend that you use a build tool that supports dependency management (such as Maven or Gradle).
 
 Maven Installation
 Spring Boot is compatible with Apache Maven 3.6.3 or later. If you do not already have Maven installed, you can follow the instructions at maven.apache.org.
 
 On many operating systems, Maven can be installed with a package manager. If you use OSX Homebrew, try brew install maven. Ubuntu users can run sudo apt-get install maven. Windows users with Chocolatey can run choco install maven from an elevated (administrator) prompt.
 Spring Boot dependencies use the org.springframework.boot group id. Typically, your Maven POM file inherits from the spring-boot-starter-parent project and declares dependencies to one or more starters. Spring Boot also provides an optional Maven plugin to create executable jars.
 
 More details on getting started with Spring Boot and Maven can be found in the Getting Started section of the Maven plugin’s reference guide.
 
 Gradle Installation
 Spring Boot is compatible with Gradle 8.x (8.14 or later) or 9.x. If you do not already have Gradle installed, you can follow the instructions at gradle.org.
 
 Spring Boot dependencies can be declared by using the org.springframework.boot group. Typically, your project declares dependencies to one or more starters. Spring Boot provides a useful Gradle plugin that can be used to simplify dependency declarations and to create executable jars.
 
 Gradle Wrapper
 The Gradle Wrapper provides a nice way of “obtaining” Gradle when you need to build a project. It is a small script and library that you commit alongside your code to bootstrap the build process. See docs.gradle.org/current/userguide/gradle_wrapper.html for details.
 
 More details on getting started with Spring Boot and Gradle can be found in the Getting Started section of the Gradle plugin’s reference guide.
 
 Installing the Spring Boot CLI
 The Spring Boot CLI (Command Line Interface) is a command line tool that you can use to quickly prototype with Spring.
 
 You do not need to use the CLI to work with Spring Boot, but it is a quick way to get a Spring application off the ground without an IDE.
 
 Manual Installation
 You can download the Spring CLI distribution from one of the following locations:
 
 spring-boot-cli-4.1.0-bin.zip
 
 spring-boot-cli-4.1.0-bin.tar.gz
 
 Once downloaded, follow the INSTALL.txt instructions from the unpacked archive. In summary, there is a spring script (spring.bat for Windows) in a bin/ directory in the .zip file. Alternatively, you can use java -jar with the .jar file (the script helps you to be sure that the classpath is set correctly).
 
 Installation with SDKMAN!
 SDKMAN! (The Software Development Kit Manager) can be used for managing multiple versions of various binary SDKs, including Groovy and the Spring Boot CLI. Get SDKMAN! from sdkman.io and install Spring Boot by using the following commands:
 
 $ sdk install springboot
 $ spring --version
 Spring CLI v4.1.0
 If you develop features for the CLI and want access to the version you built, use the following commands:
 
 $ sdk install springboot dev /path/to/spring-boot/spring-boot-cli/target/spring-boot-cli-4.1.0-bin/spring-4.1.0/
 $ sdk default springboot dev
 $ spring --version
 Spring CLI v4.1.0
 The preceding instructions install a local instance of spring called the dev instance. It points at your target build location, so every time you rebuild Spring Boot, spring is up-to-date.
 
 You can see it by running the following command:
 
 $ sdk ls springboot
 
 ================================================================================
 Available Springboot Versions
 ================================================================================
 > + dev
 * 4.1.0
 
 ================================================================================
 + - local version
 * - installed
 > - currently in use
 ================================================================================
 OSX Homebrew Installation
 If you are on a Mac and use Homebrew, you can install the Spring Boot CLI by using the following commands:
 
 $ brew tap spring-io/tap
 $ brew install spring-boot
 Homebrew installs spring to /usr/local/bin.
 
 If you do not see the formula, your installation of brew might be out-of-date. In that case, run brew update and try again.
 MacPorts Installation
 If you are on a Mac and use MacPorts, you can install the Spring Boot CLI by using the following command:
 
 $ sudo port install spring-boot-cli
 Command-line Completion
 The Spring Boot CLI includes scripts that provide command completion for the BASH and zsh shells. You can source the script named spring (_spring for zsh) or put it in your personal or system-wide bash completion initialization. On a Debian system, the system-wide scripts are in <installation location>/shell-completion/<bash|zsh> and all scripts in that directory are executed when a new shell starts. For example, to run the script manually if you have installed by using SDKMAN!, use the following commands:
 
 $ . ~/.sdkman/candidates/springboot/current/shell-completion/bash/spring
 $ spring <HIT TAB HERE>
  encodepassword help init shell version
 If you install the Spring Boot CLI by using Homebrew or MacPorts, the command-line completion scripts are automatically registered with your shell.
 Windows Scoop Installation
 If you are on a Windows and use Scoop, you can install the Spring Boot CLI by using the following commands:
 
 $ scoop bucket add extras
 $ scoop install springboot
 Scoop installs spring to ~/scoop/apps/springboot/current/bin.
 
 If you do not see the app manifest, your installation of scoop might be out-of-date. In that case, run scoop update and try again.

title: Spring: Conozca este framework de Java
text:
¿Qué es un Framework ?
 Es una herramienta ampliamente utilizada en diversas áreas de la programación, que optimiza el trabajo de los desarrolladores, centrándolo en el desarrollo de proyectos y no en los procesos de configuración y estandarización.
 
 Cabe mencionar que antes de sumergirse en un framework es recomendable que estudies y conozcas los fundamentos del lenguaje que quieres explorar. Esto hará que tu aprendizaje y desarrollo en el estudio sea más fluido. De esta manera lograrás comprender todo lo inesperado que surja.
 
 Para profundizar y saber más sobre Java, tenemos un video hablando sobre el motivo de utilizar Java actualmente.
 
 Spring Framework
 Entre muchos frameworks en el mercado como Angular, Laravel, Bootstrap e incluso Scrum, Spring es el framework más popular cuando hablamos de Java.
 
 Esta popularidad se debe principalmente a que Spring nació con la intención de hacer que la programación en Java fuera más rápida, fácil y segura, optimizando el trabajo de desarrollo. Y a quién no le gustan las herramientas que facilitan el trabajo, ¿verdad?
 
 Con Spring, se puede tener un mayor dominio del proyecto que se está desarrollando, con la característica principal de soportar la infraestructura directamente en la aplicación, permitiendo así que los equipos de desarrollo se enfoquen en la parte lógica de la aplicación, sin necesidad de preocuparse innecesariamente por cuestiones de configuración en el entorno.
 
 Puede consultar más detalles sobre Spring en el artículo que habla de cómo comenzar a utilizar el framework Spring.
 
 Pero, ¿qué beneficio realmente trajo Spring?
 Gestión de dependencias mediante inyección de dependencias
 Supongamos que creamos una aplicación Java con algunas Clases y las subimos al sistema.
 
 Los objetos de estas Clases se instanciarán en la memoria y estas Clases tendrán alguna relación entre sí. Por lo tanto, después de cada inicio de la aplicación, se realiza la red de conexiones entre objetos, utilizando referencias a estos objetos. Esto no es más que la lógica de negocios creada durante el desarrollo. ¡Perfecto!
 
 Supongamos que en este sistema tenemos una clase Alumno y una clase ForoService, que publica preguntas en el foro. Para usar los métodos de clase ForoService dentro de la clase Alumno, podemos instanciar esta clase dentro de un método de Alumno.
 
 public class Alumno { 
 public publicaMensaje (String titulo, String duda) { 
  ForoService publicaDuda = new ForoService(); 
  publicaDuda.enviaDuda(titulo, duda); 
 }
 }
 ¿Esto es malo? ¡Mucho!
 Pensemos en un escenario macro. Mantener o cambiar las reglas de negocio sería mucho trabajo, ya que entraríamos Clase por Clase para hacer estos cambios, tal es la dependencia que tiene la Clase Alumno directamente de la Clase ForoService.
 
 Diagrama con el primer componente con el título 'Clase Alumno' conectado, por el extremo derecho, con una flecha punteada hacia el segundo y último componente con el título 'Clase FórumService'
 
 Como regla, una Clase de alto nivel no puede depender de una Clase de bajo nivel, en lugar de abstracciones.
 
 En este caso, podemos delegar en Spring que gestione estas instancias de objetos para que no sea responsabilidad de lo que está desarrollando la aplicación. Por ejemplo: una aplicación en la que, en el contexto general, se administra con Spring. Cada vez que se inicien, las Clases, sean cuales sean, se le pedirá a Spring las instancias necesarias.
 
 Conectividad de base de datos
 Este módulo de Spring nos permite trabajar más fácilmente utilizando las características de la base de datos. A través de él, las tecnologías de acceso a datos y los procesos de bases de datos relacionales y no relacionales se integran de forma más directa, minimizando la pérdida de tiempo con las configuraciones, manteniendo las características de almacenamiento.
 
 Spring Data es un módulo muy completo, que cuenta con varios submódulos específicos para actuar en determinados bancos. Esta división y especificación permite el uso de módulos más adecuados para el banco elegido, lo que ortoga un mayor control sobre la aplicación en el proyecto con las particularidades que cada uno demanda.
 
 Una de las formas más utilizadas para conectarse a una base de datos, por mucho tiempo, fue el famoso JDBC. Sin embargo, funcionaba solo teniendo algunas dificultades, desde la conectividad hasta una implementación en la búsqueda de información en la base de datos.
 
 Hoy, Spring Framework nos ofrece la posibilidad de usar Spring Data para que no tengamos que usar toda esta estructura JDBC detrás de escena. En cambio, es más fácil comunicarse con cualquier base de datos, como MySQL, Postgrees u otros procesadores de datos.
 
 Aplicaciones web
 Spring MVC surgió como una evolución de Java EE para facilitar el trabajo de las personas que desarrollan aplicaciones web. Este módulo tiene todas las características que necesitamos para desarrollar aplicaciones robustas y flexibles, por lo que no tenemos que preocuparnos por configuraciones como EJB, EJB con Jakarta EE, JSF, integración con CDI y otras necesidades de Java EE.
 
 Muchas aplicaciones web necesitan una forma dinámica de manejar páginas HTML, CSS, Javascript y aquí tenemos Spring MVC que ofrece todas estas facilidades. Le permite desarrollar fácilmente aplicaciones web y Rest API utilizando el mismo marco de inyección de dependencia.
 
 Seguridad en tus aplicaciones
 Spring Security se enfoca en proporcionar un marco de autenticación robusto y, al mismo tiempo, altamente personalizable. A través de él podemos proteger las aplicaciones de Spring.
 
 Con el objetivo de la seguridad, este módulo se enfoca en brindar autenticación y autorización a las aplicaciones, destacando la facilidad de adaptar sus requerimientos para cumplir con las variadas demandas y requerimientos de los proyectos que necesitarán utilizarlo.
 
 ¿Cómo puedo usar Spring Framework con Java?
 Hemos hablado mucho sobre el uso de Spring como marco de Java, pero no es solo este lenguaje el que se destaca . Kotlin es un lenguaje de programación moderno, conciso y seguro que ha sido ampliamente utilizado por los desarrolladores para Android e incluso iOS como una opción para Swift y desde Spring Boot versión 2.2, Kotlin se ha integrado al 100% en el marco.
 
 Kotlin es famoso en el desarrollo de aplicaciones móviles, sin embargo, también se utiliza para desarrollar aplicaciones web o desktop.
 
 ¿Cómo usar Spring Framework con Java?
 En este artículo conocemos el concepto de framework y cómo podemos desarrollarlo día a día, facilitando y agilizando los procesos de trabajo.
 
 Avanzando en el conocimiento de los frameworks, conocemos Spring, el favorito de los que trabajan con Java. Así entendemos cómo el proceso de desarrollo esta más centrado en el propio código, asimismo aprendimos un poco sobre algunos de sus módulos más utilizados.
 
 Finalmente, descubrimos la versatilidad de Spring que, además de usarse en proyectos Java, también puede ser una excelente opción para aquellas personas que quieran desarrollar aplicaciones usando Kotlin.

title: Building an Application with Spring Boot
Building a RESTful Web Service with Spring Boot Actuator
text:
Spring Boot Actuator is a subproject of Spring Boot that adds production-ready features to applications with minimal configuration. It is mainly used to monitor, manage, and expose operational information about a running Spring Boot application. Actuator provides built-in endpoints such as health checks, application information, metrics, and management features that help operate applications in production environments.
 
 A typical Spring Boot Actuator application starts by creating a Spring Boot project with dependencies such as Spring Web and Spring Boot Actuator, usually through Spring Initializr. The main application class uses the @SpringBootApplication annotation and starts the application through SpringApplication.run(). This annotation enables important Spring Boot features, including automatic configuration, component scanning, and configuration of the embedded web server.
 
 Spring Boot automatically configures many components based on the project dependencies. For example, when spring-webmvc is available, Spring Boot enables Spring MVC features and configures the required infrastructure, including an embedded servlet container such as Tomcat. This allows developers to create REST APIs without manually configuring servers or XML files.
 
 REST endpoints in Spring Boot are created using Spring MVC controllers. A class annotated with @RestController defines HTTP endpoints that return data directly in the response body instead of rendering views. An endpoint such as @GetMapping("/hello-world") can receive HTTP GET requests and return Java objects that are automatically converted into JSON responses using message converters such as Jackson.
 
 Spring Boot applications commonly use representation classes to model API responses. These classes contain the data structure returned by REST endpoints, such as an object with fields like id and content. When a controller returns this object, Spring Boot converts it into JSON automatically, allowing the application to expose RESTful services easily.
 
 Spring Boot Actuator adds management endpoints under the /actuator path. For example, /actuator/health provides the current health status of the application, returning information such as {"status":"UP"} when the application is running correctly. These endpoints are useful for monitoring systems, cloud platforms, and deployment environments because they provide information about application availability.
 
 Spring Boot applications can be packaged as executable JAR files that include the application code, dependencies, and embedded server. These JAR files can be executed using java -jar, making deployment simpler across different environments. Applications can also be executed during development using Maven commands such as mvn spring-boot:run or Gradle commands such as gradle bootRun.
 
 The server ports used by Spring Boot and Actuator can be customized through configuration files such as application.properties. For example, the main application can run on one port while management endpoints run on another using properties like server.port and management.server.port.
 
 Spring Boot Actuator applications should include tests to verify that REST controllers and management endpoints work correctly. Spring Boot provides testing support through annotations such as @SpringBootTest, allowing developers to start the application context and validate HTTP responses.
 
 Spring Boot Actuator is an essential component for production-grade backend applications because it provides observability, health monitoring, and operational management while maintaining the simplicity and automatic configuration principles of Spring Boot.

title: Spring Boot
text:
Spring Boot is a framework built on top of the Spring ecosystem that helps developers create production-grade Java applications and services with minimal configuration. Its main objective is to simplify Spring development by providing sensible default configurations, reducing the amount of setup required while still allowing developers to customize the application when needed.
 
 Spring Boot follows an opinionated approach: it automatically configures many components based on the project dependencies and application requirements, allowing developers to focus more on business logic instead of infrastructure configuration. At the same time, Spring Boot does not restrict customization, and developers can override default behaviors when their application requires different configurations.
 
 Spring Boot can be used to create standalone Java applications that run directly with java -jar, as well as traditional WAR deployments for application servers. It also provides a command-line tool that allows developers to run Spring scripts quickly.
 
 One of the main advantages of Spring Boot is that it provides production-ready features commonly required in backend applications. These features include embedded servers, security configuration, metrics, health checks, and externalized configuration. By including these capabilities as part of the framework, Spring Boot simplifies the process of creating applications ready for real-world deployment.
 
 A basic Spring Boot application can be created using the @SpringBootApplication annotation and the SpringApplication.run() method. The @SpringBootApplication annotation enables important Spring Boot features such as automatic configuration and component scanning. The application can expose REST endpoints using Spring MVC annotations like @RestController and @RequestMapping, allowing developers to create web services with very little code.
 
 Spring Boot avoids unnecessary complexity by eliminating the need for XML configuration and avoiding code generation. Instead, it dynamically configures the application at startup based on dependencies, annotations, and configuration properties.
 
 The Spring Boot ecosystem includes additional modules and tools that extend its capabilities. For example, Spring Boot Actuator provides monitoring and management endpoints, while Spring Initializr helps developers generate project templates with the required dependencies and configuration.
 
 Spring Boot applications can be built using modern Java development tools such as Maven or Gradle. Developers can run applications directly during development or package them as executable JAR files for deployment. Spring Boot supports production environments by providing features that improve observability, maintainability, and operational management.
 
 Spring Boot is widely used in backend development with Java because it accelerates application creation while maintaining the flexibility and power of the Spring Framework. It is commonly used for building REST APIs, microservices, enterprise applications, and cloud-native services.
 
 Keywords: Spring Boot, Java backend, Spring Framework, REST API, auto-configuration, embedded server, executable JAR, Actuator, Maven, Gradle, production-ready applications.

title: Django at a glance
text:
Django is a high-level Python web framework designed to make the development of database-driven web applications fast, secure, and maintainable. It provides built-in tools for common backend tasks such as database management, URL routing, request handling, HTML rendering, and administrative interfaces. Django follows the MVT (Model-View-Template) architecture, which separates application responsibilities: • Model: Defines the data structure and database interaction. • View: Handles requests, executes business logic, and returns responses. • Template: Defines the presentation layer using dynamic HTML generation. Django ORM (Object-Relational Mapper) Django includes a built-in ORM that allows developers to define database structures using Python classes instead of writing SQL directly. Models represent database tables, while class attributes represent fields: from django.db import models class Reporter(models.Model): full_name = models.CharField(max_length=70) class Article(models.Model): headline = models.CharField(max_length=200) content = models.TextField() reporter = models.ForeignKey(Reporter, on_delete=models.CASCADE) The ORM provides: • Database abstraction through Python objects. • Relationships between models. • Automatic SQL generation. • CRUD operations without manually writing queries. Examples: Reporter.objects.all() Reporter.objects.get(id=1) Article.objects.filter(reporter__full_name__startswith="John") Database migrations Django manages database schema changes through migrations. Main commands: python manage.py makemigrations python manage.py migrate • makemigrations detects changes in models and creates migration files. • migrate applies those changes to the database. Migrations allow developers to evolve database structures while keeping changes tracked and reproducible. Django Admin Interface Django can automatically generate a production-ready administration panel from defined models. By registering models: from django.contrib import admin from . import models admin.site.register(models.Article) Developers get an interface where authenticated users can: • Create records. • Update data. • Delete objects. • Manage application content. This reduces the need to manually build internal management dashboards. URL Routing (URLconf) Django uses URL configuration files to map HTTP paths to Python functions. Example: urlpatterns = [ path("articles//", views.year_archive), path("articles///", views.month_archive), ] The routing system: • Matches incoming requests. • Extracts parameters from URLs. • Calls the corresponding view function. Example request: /articles/2005/05/ can call: views.month_archive(request, year=2005, month=5) Views Views contain the application logic that processes requests and returns responses. Example: def year_archive(request, year): articles = Article.objects.filter(pub_date__year=year) context = { "year": year, "article_list": articles } return render(request, "news/year_archive.html", context) Views commonly: • Receive HTTP requests. • Query data through models. • Prepare response data. • Render templates or return API responses. Templates Django templates generate dynamic HTML pages. Example: {% for article in article_list %}

{{ article.headline }}

{% endfor %} Features: • Variable rendering. • Template inheritance. • Filters. • Reusable layouts. Template inheritance allows sharing common structures: {% extends "base.html" %} This avoids repeating HTML code across pages. Main Django Features Django provides several built-in capabilities: • Object-Relational Mapping (ORM). • Database migrations. • Automatic admin interface. • URL routing. • Template engine. • Authentication system. • Security protections. • Caching framework. • RSS and Atom feed generation.

title: Writing your first Django app, part 1
text:
Django is a Python web framework designed to simplify the development of web applications by providing a structured environment with built-in tools for configuration, routing, database management, administration, and application organization. A Django project represents the complete configuration of a website, including global settings, URL definitions, and installed applications. In contrast, a Django application is a modular component that performs a specific function, such as managing polls, users, products, or blog content. A single project can contain multiple applications, and applications can be reused in different projects, which encourages modular and maintainable software design.
 
 The first step when working with Django is verifying the installation using python -m django --version. Once Django is available, a new project can be created with the command django-admin startproject. This command generates the basic structure required for a Django website, including important files such as manage.py, settings.py, urls.py, asgi.py, and wsgi.py. The manage.py file provides a command-line interface for managing the project, allowing developers to execute operations such as starting the development server, creating applications, and applying database migrations. The settings.py file contains the configuration of the Django project, including database settings, installed applications, middleware, and other framework options. The urls.py file defines the main URL routing system, while asgi.py and wsgi.py provide entry points for deployment using compatible web servers.
 
 Django includes a lightweight development server that can be started with python manage.py runserver. This server is intended for local development and testing, allowing developers to quickly see changes without configuring a production environment. It provides automatic code reloading when Python files are modified, which improves the development workflow. However, Django’s built-in server is not designed for production use because production environments require specialized web servers and deployment configurations.
 
 After creating the project, developers usually create applications using python manage.py startapp. Django automatically generates a standard application structure containing files such as models.py, views.py, admin.py, and a migrations directory. The models.py file defines the data structures that interact with the database, views.py contains the logic that processes requests and generates responses, admin.py configures the administrative interface, and migrations store changes related to database structure. This organization allows developers to separate responsibilities and build applications that are easier to maintain, extend, and reuse.

title: Writing your first Django app, part 1
text:
Django handles web requests through a structured process that connects URLs, views, models, templates, and responses. A view is a Python function or class responsible for receiving an HTTP request and returning an HTTP response. The request object contains information about the client request, while response objects such as HttpResponse provide the content returned to the browser. Views represent the main point where application logic is executed, including retrieving information, processing user actions, and deciding what response should be generated.
 
 To make views accessible through a browser, Django uses URL configuration files known as URLconf. A URLconf creates a relationship between URL patterns and Python functions. Each Django application can define its own urls.py file, allowing application-specific routes to remain independent from the main project configuration. The project-level urls.py file can connect application routes using the include() function, which delegates part of the URL processing to another URL configuration. This approach improves organization because applications can be moved, reused, or integrated into different projects without changing their internal routing logic.
 
 The Django request lifecycle follows a clear sequence. When a user accesses a URL, Django receives the HTTP request and searches for a matching route in the URL configuration. Once a matching pattern is found, Django calls the associated view. The view can retrieve or modify data through models, process application logic, and return a response. If templates are used, the view sends data to the template system, which generates the final HTML content displayed to the user.
 
 Django follows the Model-View-Template (MVT) architectural pattern. Models represent the data layer and define how information is stored and accessed in the database. Views represent the application logic layer and control how requests are handled. Templates represent the presentation layer and define how information is displayed to users. This separation allows developers to maintain cleaner code by keeping database operations, business logic, and interface design independent.
 
 Understanding Django’s project structure, URL routing system, views, and MVT architecture provides the foundation required to build scalable web applications. These concepts allow developers to organize code efficiently, create reusable components, and develop applications that can grow from simple prototypes into complete production systems.

title: Writing your first Django app, part 2
text:
Django provides a powerful database abstraction layer that allows developers to define application data structures using Python classes instead of writing database schemas manually. The main database configuration is located in the settings.py file through the DATABASES setting. By default, Django uses SQLite because it requires no additional installation and is suitable for learning and small projects. For production environments, developers often choose more scalable databases such as PostgreSQL.
 
 The INSTALLED_APPS setting defines which Django applications are active inside a project. These applications can provide models, authentication systems, administrative interfaces, sessions, static file management, and other reusable functionality. Django applications are designed to be reusable and can be installed across multiple projects.
