 Django uses migrations to manage changes between application models and the database schema. The migration system tracks modifications made to models and converts them into database operations. The command python manage.py makemigrations creates migration files that describe changes, while python manage.py migrate applies those changes to the database. This approach allows developers to evolve database structures over time without manually recreating tables or losing existing data.
 
 Models are the foundation of Django’s data layer. A model is a Python class that inherits from django.db.models.Model and represents a database table. Each class attribute defines a database field, such as CharField for text values, DateTimeField for dates and times, and IntegerField for numeric values. Django automatically generates database tables, primary keys, and SQL statements based on these model definitions.
 
 Django follows the DRY (Don’t Repeat Yourself) principle by keeping the data definition in one central location: the model. From the model structure, Django can automatically create migrations, generate database schemas, and provide an API for interacting with stored data.
 
 Relationships between models are defined using fields such as ForeignKey, which represents many-to-one relationships. For example, a polling application may contain a Question model and a Choice model, where multiple choices belong to a single question. Django supports common database relationships, including one-to-one, many-to-one, and many-to-many relationships.
 
 A typical workflow for modifying database structures in Django is:
 
 Update models in models.py.
 Run python manage.py makemigrations to generate migration files.
 Run python manage.py migrate to apply changes to the database.
 
 This migration-based approach provides version control for database changes and enables teams to safely maintain evolving applications across development and production environments

title: Writing your first Django app, part 2
text:
Django includes an Object-Relational Mapper (ORM) that allows developers to interact with databases using Python objects instead of writing SQL queries directly. After defining models, Django automatically generates a database API that supports creating, reading, updating, and deleting records through model objects.
 
 The ORM is accessed through the model manager, commonly using objects. Developers can retrieve data with methods such as all(), filter(), and get(). For example, Question.objects.all() returns all stored questions, while Question.objects.filter() allows searching records using specific conditions. Django converts these Python queries into optimized SQL operations internally.
 
 Django’s ORM supports advanced queries through field lookups using the double underscore syntax (__). This allows developers to filter data based on field conditions or navigate through relationships between models. For example, queries can search records by text patterns, dates, related objects, or multiple conditions without manually writing SQL joins.
 
 The ORM automatically manages relationships between objects. When a model contains a ForeignKey, Django creates methods that allow navigation between related objects. For example, a Question object can access all related Choice objects through a reverse relationship, while each Choice can access its associated Question.
 
 Models can also contain custom methods to add application-specific behavior. The __str__() method defines the human-readable representation of an object, improving readability in the interactive shell and Django administration interface. Custom methods can also implement business logic directly inside the model.
 
 Django provides an automatic administration interface designed for internal users such as administrators, content managers, or staff members. Instead of manually building management dashboards, developers can register models in admin.py, and Django automatically generates forms, lists, editing pages, and validation logic.
 
 To access the admin interface, developers create an administrator account using:
 
 python manage.py createsuperuser
 
 After registering models with:
 
 admin.site.register(ModelName)
 
 Django makes those models available inside the administration panel. The admin interface automatically detects model fields and generates appropriate HTML input controls, including date pickers and validation behavior.
 
 The Django admin system separates content management from the public application. It allows authorized users to manage database records efficiently while developers focus on building the user-facing features of the application. This combination of ORM capabilities and automatic administration makes Django highly productive for building database-driven web applications.

title: Writing your first Django app, part 3
text:
Django views are the core component responsible for processing web requests and returning responses. A view represents a type of web page or application behavior and is usually implemented as a Python function or class-based view. When a user accesses a URL, Django uses URL configuration files (URLconf) to determine which view should handle the request. This separation allows applications to maintain clean and flexible URL structures while keeping business logic inside views.
 
 A Django URLconf maps URL patterns to views using the path() function. URL patterns can capture dynamic values from the URL and pass them as arguments to the view. For example, a pattern such as path("<int:question_id>/", views.detail) captures an integer value from the URL and sends it as the question_id parameter to the detail() view. Django processes URL patterns in order, finds the first matching pattern, and calls the associated view function with the request object and captured parameters.
 
 Views are responsible for returning an HttpResponse object or raising an exception such as Http404. A view can retrieve data from the database, process user input, generate files, render templates, or perform any required application logic. Django encourages separating presentation from logic by using templates instead of generating HTML directly inside Python code.
 
 The template system allows views to pass data to HTML files through a context dictionary. Templates use Django Template Language syntax, including variables ({{ variable }}), loops ({% for %}), conditions ({% if %}), and filters. This approach keeps application logic separate from the user interface and makes templates easier to maintain. The render() shortcut simplifies the common workflow of loading a template, providing context data, and returning an HttpResponse.
 
 Django provides helper functions to simplify common view operations. The get_object_or_404() shortcut retrieves an object from the database and automatically raises an HTTP 404 error if the object does not exist. This keeps views cleaner while maintaining separation between the model and view layers.
 
 URL naming is another important Django practice. Instead of hardcoding URLs directly inside templates, developers should use named URL patterns and the {% url %} template tag. This allows URLs to change without requiring updates across multiple templates. For larger projects containing multiple applications, Django supports URL namespaces using app_name, preventing conflicts between similarly named views.
 
 Overall, Django views, URLconfs, and templates form the foundation of Django’s Model-View-Template architecture. URLs define how requests are routed, views handle application behavior, and templates control presentation. This structure promotes reusable, maintainable, and scalable web applications.

title: Writing your first Django app, part 4
text:
Django form processing allows applications to receive user input, validate submitted data, modify database records, and return appropriate responses. HTML forms that change server-side data should use the POST method instead of GET, because POST requests are designed for operations that modify application state. Django provides built-in protection against Cross-Site Request Forgery (CSRF) attacks through the {% csrf_token %} template tag, which should be included in internal POST forms.
 
 In a Django application, a form submission sends data through the request.POST object, which behaves like a dictionary containing submitted values. Views can retrieve specific fields, process the information, update models, and redirect users after successful operations. For example, a voting application can retrieve the selected option ID from request.POST["choice"], update the corresponding database record, and display updated results.
 
 Django recommends returning an HttpResponseRedirect after successfully processing POST data. This pattern, commonly known as the Post/Redirect/Get (PRG) pattern, prevents users from accidentally submitting the same form multiple times when refreshing or navigating backward. Django’s reverse() function helps generate URLs dynamically from named URL patterns instead of hardcoding paths inside views, making applications easier to maintain when URL structures change.
 
 Database updates can be optimized using Django’s database expressions. The F() expression allows operations to be performed directly at the database level. For example, increasing a vote counter with F("votes") + 1 avoids unnecessary data retrieval and reduces the risk of incorrect updates when multiple users interact with the application simultaneously.
 
 As Django applications grow, repetitive view logic can become difficult to maintain. Generic views provide reusable abstractions for common development patterns, reducing the amount of custom Python code required. Django includes generic views such as ListView for displaying collections of objects and DetailView for displaying individual objects. These classes automatically handle common tasks like retrieving objects, selecting templates, and creating context variables.
 
 To use generic views, developers define classes that inherit from Django’s generic view classes and specify the related model or customize methods such as get_queryset(). The model attribute tells Django which database model the view should use, while template_name allows developers to select a specific template instead of Django’s default naming conventions. The context_object_name attribute can customize the variable name sent to templates.
 
 Generic views follow Django’s philosophy of reducing repetitive code while keeping applications organized. They are especially useful for standard CRUD-style applications where users frequently list, view, create, update, or delete database objects. By combining forms, request handling, URL routing, and generic views, Django provides a powerful structure for building maintainable and scalable web applications.

title: Writing your first Django app, part 5
text:
Automated tests are routines that verify that an application works as expected. They can be used to check small parts of a program, such as whether a model method returns the correct value, or larger parts of the system, such as whether user actions produce the expected results. Unlike manual testing, where developers must repeatedly check the application themselves, automated tests run these checks automatically after they have been created. This allows developers to make changes with more confidence because they can quickly verify that existing functionality has not been broken.
 
 Tests become especially important as an application grows. A change in one part of the code can create unexpected problems in another part of the system. Automated tests help detect these issues quickly and make it easier to identify the source of a problem. They also prevent bugs from returning because once a problem has been converted into a test, future executions of the test suite will warn developers if the same error appears again. Tests also improve collaboration because they document the expected behavior of the application and help different developers modify the same project without accidentally breaking existing features.
 
 Django provides tools to create automated tests through the django.test.TestCase class. Tests are usually placed in the application’s tests.py file, where Django automatically discovers them. A common testing process is to identify a bug, create a test that reproduces the incorrect behavior, modify the code to fix the issue, and then run the test again to confirm that the solution works.
 
 In the polls application, a problem was found in the Question.was_published_recently() method. The method was supposed to return True only when a question had been published within the last day, but it also returned True when the publication date was in the future. A test was created to verify that a question with a future pub_date should return False. When the test was executed with python manage.py test polls, Django created a testing database, found the test case, executed it, and reported the failure because the method returned an incorrect value.
 
 The issue was fixed by changing the method so that the publication date must be between one day ago and the current time. Additional tests were added to verify three possible situations: old questions should not be considered recent, recently published questions should return True, and future questions should return `False. This created a stronger guarantee that the method would continue working correctly after future changes.
 
 Django also provides a test client that simulates requests from a user’s browser. It can be used to test views, responses, status codes, templates, and returned data. In the polls application, the index view originally displayed questions that had future publication dates. The get_queryset() method was updated to filter questions using timezone.now(), ensuring that only published questions appear. Tests were then created to verify different scenarios, including no questions, past questions, future questions, and combinations of both.
 
 Testing views also requires protecting detail pages. Even if future questions are hidden from the index page, users could still access them directly through their URLs. The DetailView was modified to exclude unpublished questions, and tests confirmed that past questions are accessible while future questions return a 404 Not Found response.
 
 As applications become larger, tests should continue growing with the project. Good practices include creating separate test classes for different models or views, writing individual test methods for specific conditions, and using descriptive names. Tools such as Selenium can extend testing by checking browser behavior, HTML rendering, and JavaScript interactions. Automated testing is an essential part of Django development because it improves reliability, prevents regressions, and helps maintain software quality over time.

title: Writing your first Django app, part 6
Writing your first Django app, part 7
text:
Django provides an automatically generated administration interface that allows developers and administrators to manage application data through a web interface. By default, registering a model with admin.site.register() creates a basic admin form, but Django allows extensive customization through ModelAdmin classes.
 A common customization is modifying the structure and appearance of admin forms. Instead of directly registering a model, developers can create a custom admin class and pass it as the second argument to admin.site.register(). The fields option controls the order of fields displayed in the form, while fieldsets allows grouping fields into sections with titles. This improves usability when models contain many fields.
 Django also supports managing related objects directly from a model’s admin page. For example, a Question model with related Choice objects can use inline administration. StackedInline displays related objects vertically, while TabularInline presents them in a compact table format. The extra option controls how many empty forms for related objects are displayed by default.
 The admin list view can also be customized to improve data management. The list_display option defines which model fields or methods appear as columns in the object list. Custom methods can be displayed using the @admin.display() decorator, which allows configuration of column names, sorting behavior, and boolean display. The list_filter option adds filtering controls based on model fields, while search_fields enables searching through selected fields.
 Django’s admin interface is built using Django templates, which means it can be visually customized by overriding default admin templates. Developers can create a project-level templates directory, configure it through the TEMPLATES setting, and replace default admin templates such as admin/base_site.html. This allows changing elements like the administration site title, branding, and layout.
 Template organization follows similar principles to static files: application-specific templates should remain inside the application when they belong only to that app, while project-wide customizations can be stored in a shared templates directory. Django automatically discovers templates from installed applications when APP_DIRS is enabled.
 Customizing Django Admin improves the usability, organization, and maintainability of administrative interfaces. Through ModelAdmin, inline models, list customization, filters, search capabilities, and template overrides, developers can adapt the default admin system to match the needs of more complex applications.

title: Django
text:
Django projects are organized into two main concepts: projects and applications. A project contains the global configuration for a website, including settings, database configuration, and URL routing. An application is a component that performs a specific function, such as a blog, a poll system, or a database interface. A single project can contain multiple applications, and applications can be reused across different projects.
 
 The first step when creating a Django project is generating the initial project structure using the django-admin startproject command. This creates important files such as manage.py, which provides a command-line interface for interacting with the project, and the project package containing configuration files.
 
 The main configuration files include settings.py, which stores project settings such as installed applications and database configuration; urls.py, which defines the URL routing table; asgi.py and wsgi.py, which provide entry points for web servers; and __init__.py, which identifies the directory as a Python package.
 
 After creating the project, Django provides a development server that can be started with python manage.py runserver. This lightweight server allows developers to test applications locally without configuring a production server. It includes automatic reloading, meaning that many code changes are detected automatically during development. However, this server is intended only for development and should not be used in production environments.
 
 Django applications are created using the python manage.py startapp command. This generates the standard application structure, including files such as models.py for database models, views.py for application logic, admin.py for administration configuration, tests.py for automated tests, and a migrations directory for database changes.
 
 The request-response flow in Django begins with URL configuration. A view is a Python function that receives a request and returns a response. To make a view accessible through a browser, it must be connected to a URL pattern. Applications commonly define their own urls.py file and then connect it to the main project URL configuration using include().
 
 The path() function maps a URL route to a view, while include() allows Django to delegate URL handling to another URL configuration. This structure keeps applications independent and reusable because each app manages its own routes.
 
 By creating a simple view, defining application URLs, and connecting them to the main project, developers establish the basic Django workflow: a browser request reaches the URL configuration, Django selects the appropriate view, and the view returns an HTTP response.
 
 This foundation introduces the core structure of Django development and prepares the application for more advanced features such as database models, templates, forms, testing, and administration customization.

title: Node.js v26.5.1 documentation Assert
text:
The node:assert module provides a collection of assertion functions used to verify conditions during testing and internal validation in Node.js applications. Its primary purpose is to ensure that values meet expected conditions, throwing an AssertionError whenever an assertion fails. The module supports two assertion modes: strict and legacy. In strict mode, comparison methods perform strict equality checks, and methods such as deepEqual() behave the same as deepStrictEqual(), producing detailed diffs that highlight differences between actual and expected values. Legacy mode exists for backward compatibility and relies on type-coercive comparisons using the == operator, which can lead to unexpected behavior and is generally discouraged in modern applications.
 
 Assertion methods accept optional custom messages that can be provided as strings, Error instances, or functions that generate messages only when an assertion fails. When an Error object is supplied, it is thrown directly instead of creating a new AssertionError. The AssertionError class extends the standard Error class and includes additional information such as the actual value, expected value, comparison operator, the ERR_ASSERTION error code, and an indicator showing whether the error message was generated automatically. Node.js also provides the Assert class, which allows developers to create independent assertion instances with configurable behavior, including strict mode, full or simplified diff output, and optional prototype comparison through the skipPrototype setting.
 
 The module includes methods for both shallow and deep equality comparisons. Functions such as strictEqual() use Object.is() to compare primitive values strictly, while deepStrictEqual() recursively compares nested objects, prototypes, symbols, collections such as Map and Set, and special objects including Error and RegExp. Complementary methods such as notStrictEqual() and notDeepStrictEqual() verify inequality, whereas legacy methods like equal() and deepEqual() remain available for compatibility but are not recommended because they rely on implicit type coercion. Additional assertion utilities include match() and doesNotMatch() for validating regular expressions, throws() and doesNotThrow() for verifying synchronous exceptions, rejects() and doesNotReject() for asynchronous promise validation, fail() for explicitly triggering assertion failures, ifError() for validating callback errors, and partialDeepStrictEqual() for comparing only the expected subset of object properties. Together, these APIs form the foundation of Node.js's built-in assertion system for unit testing and runtime validation.

title: Node.js
text:
Node.js is an open-source, cross-platform JavaScript runtime environment designed to execute JavaScript applications outside the browser. It provides the runtime necessary to build server-side applications, command-line tools, networking services, and other scalable software using JavaScript. The project follows an open development model and publishes official documentation for every released version, allowing developers to reference APIs and features that correspond to the version of Node.js they are using.
 
 Node.js follows Semantic Versioning (SemVer) and distributes releases through multiple release channels that balance new feature development with long-term stability. The Current release line represents the actively developed version of Node.js and receives the latest features, improvements, and major changes. A new major version is released approximately every six months, typically in April and October, allowing the platform to evolve while introducing breaking changes only during major version updates. Current releases are intended for developers who want access to the newest capabilities and are willing to adopt the latest platform changes.
 
 The Long Term Support (LTS) release line focuses on stability, reliability, and security for production environments. Every even-numbered major release eventually becomes an LTS release after an initial development period. LTS versions receive an initial phase of Active LTS support, during which bug fixes, performance improvements, and security updates are delivered, followed by a Maintenance phase that continues providing critical fixes without introducing breaking changes or significant new features. Because of this predictable support lifecycle, LTS releases are generally recommended for production systems and enterprise applications.
 
 Node.js also provides Nightly releases, which are automatically generated builds from the Current development branch whenever changes are made. These builds allow developers to test the latest code and upcoming features before official releases but should be used with caution because they may contain unstable or experimental functionality.
 
 Official API documentation is published for both the latest Current release and individual Node.js versions, enabling developers to consult documentation that matches the runtime they are using. This versioned documentation helps maintain compatibility across projects and ensures that developers can accurately reference APIs, features, and behavioral differences between Node.js releases while following the platform's release and support lifecycle.

title: Modules: CommonJS modules
text:
CommonJS is the original module system used by Node.js to organize and share JavaScript code across multiple files. In the CommonJS model, every file is treated as an independent module with its own private scope. Variables declared inside a module are not accessible from other modules unless they are explicitly exported. This isolation is achieved by wrapping every module in a function before execution, allowing top-level variables to remain local while providing module-specific objects such as exports, module, require, __filename, and __dirname.
 
 Modules expose functionality by assigning properties to the exports object or by replacing module.exports with a new object, function, or class. While exports acts as a convenient reference to module.exports, assigning a new value directly to exports breaks that connection and does not change what the module exports. For this reason, replacing an entire module interface should always be done through module.exports, whereas adding individual properties can be accomplished using exports.property = value.
 
 Modules are imported using the require() function, which loads the exported contents of another module. A module can import local files using relative paths such as ./module or ../module, built-in Node.js modules such as node:fs, or third-party packages installed in node_modules. Each module is executed only once during the application's lifetime, after which its exported object is cached and reused by subsequent require() calls. This caching mechanism improves performance and allows multiple modules to share the same exported instance without re-executing the module code.
 
 Node.js supports both CommonJS modules and ECMAScript Modules (ESM). By default, files with the .cjs extension are treated as CommonJS modules, while .mjs files are interpreted as ECMAScript modules. Files using the .js extension are interpreted according to the nearest package.json file and its "type" field, allowing projects to explicitly choose between "commonjs" and "module". Although both module systems coexist in modern Node.js, require() always uses the CommonJS loader, whereas import uses the ECMAScript module loader. Understanding the relationship between require(), exports, module.exports, and the module scope is fundamental for developing modular Node.js applications and for maintaining compatibility between CommonJS and ECMAScript module ecosystems.

title: Modules: CommonJS modules
text:
Node.js supports two module systems: CommonJS (CJS) and ECMAScript Modules (ESM). The module system used for a file is determined by its file extension and the nearest package.json configuration. Files with the .cjs extension are always treated as CommonJS modules, while files with the .mjs extension are always treated as ECMAScript modules. Files with the .js extension are interpreted according to the nearest package.json file. If the "type" field is set to "commonjs", .js files are loaded as CommonJS modules. If the "type" field is set to "module", .js files are interpreted as ECMAScript modules. When no "type" field is present, Node.js applies its default detection rules, although package authors are encouraged to explicitly specify the module type to improve compatibility with build tools, loaders, and other development utilities.
 
 The CommonJS module loader is used whenever code imports dependencies through the require() function, while the ECMAScript module loader is used for the import statement and the dynamic import() function. These loaders follow different resolution and execution rules, making it important to understand which module system a project uses. Although CommonJS and ECMAScript Modules can coexist within the same application, interoperability between them depends on specific compatibility rules implemented by Node.js.
 
 When a CommonJS file is executed directly using the node command, the require.main property references the current module, allowing code to determine whether it is being executed as the application's entry point or imported by another module. Comparing require.main === module is a common pattern for detecting direct execution. If the file is loaded through require(), this comparison evaluates to false because another module is acting as the application's entry point. When the entry point is an ECMAScript module, require.main is undefined because the CommonJS module loader is not responsible for loading the application.
 
 Understanding how Node.js determines the active module system is essential for organizing projects, configuring package.json, selecting the appropriate import syntax, and ensuring compatibility between CommonJS and ECMAScript Modules. Explicitly defining the module type helps avoid ambiguity and provides predictable behavior across development tools, runtime environments, and package ecosystems.

title: Modules: CommonJS modules
text:
The require() function in Node.js follows a well-defined module resolution algorithm to determine which module should be loaded for a given identifier. The resolution process depends on the format of the requested path and whether the target represents a built-in module, a local file, or a package installed in node_modules. Before loading a module, developers can use require.resolve() to determine the exact file path that require() would load without executing the module itself.
 
 When the requested identifier matches a built-in Node.js module, the built-in implementation is loaded immediately. If the identifier begins with /, Node.js interprets it as an absolute file system path. Identifiers beginning with ./, ../, or . are treated as relative paths and resolved from the directory of the calling module. During file resolution, Node.js attempts to locate an exact file match before checking supported extensions such as .js, .json, and .node. For .js files, the module system is determined by the nearest package.json and its "type" field, allowing the file to be interpreted as either CommonJS or an ECMAScript module. JSON files are parsed into JavaScript objects, while .node files are loaded as compiled native addons.
 
 If the requested path refers to a directory, Node.js attempts to resolve the module by reading the directory's package.json file and evaluating its "main" field. If no valid entry point is defined, the loader falls back to searching for default files such as index.js, index.json, or index.node. When no matching file can be found, the module resolution process terminates with a MODULE_NOT_FOUND error.
 
 For package imports that do not specify a relative or absolute path, Node.js searches for the requested package inside node_modules directories. The search begins in the current module's directory and proceeds upward through each parent directory until the root of the file system is reached. Modern package resolution also considers package metadata such as the "exports" and "imports" fields defined in package.json, enabling packages to expose controlled public entry points and internal module aliases. Package self-resolution allows a package to reference itself using its own package name, while package import maps provide additional control over internal module paths.
 
 If a module cannot be resolved as CommonJS, Node.js may attempt to detect whether the source should instead be interpreted as an ECMAScript module based on file syntax and package configuration. This detection mechanism allows the runtime to support both CommonJS and ECMAScript Modules while maintaining compatibility with existing applications. Together, these resolution rules define how Node.js consistently locates, interprets, and loads modules across local files, built-in libraries, and installed packages.

title: Modules: Packages
text:
A package in Node.js is a directory structure described by a package.json file. The package includes the directory containing that file and all of its subdirectories until another package.json file is found or a node_modules directory boundary is reached. The package.json file acts as the configuration point for how Node.js interprets and exposes the package. Among other things, it can define the package name, entry points, module system, exports, and internal import mappings.
 
 One of the most important decisions Node.js makes when loading code is determining whether a file should be interpreted as an ES module (ESM) or a CommonJS (CJS) module. Node.js uses several signals to decide this. Files ending in .mjs are always treated as ES modules. Files ending in .cjs are always treated as CommonJS modules. For .js files, the nearest parent package.json controls the behavior through the top-level "type" field. If "type": "module" is present, .js files are interpreted as ES modules. If "type": "commonjs" is present, or if the field is missing, .js files are interpreted as CommonJS.
 
 The "type" field applies not only to the initial file executed by Node.js, but also to files imported through import statements or dynamic import() expressions. For example, if a project contains a package.json with "type": "module", a file such as app.js will be loaded as an ES module, and another file imported from it, such as ./startup/init.js, will also inherit that module interpretation unless another closer package.json changes the behavior.
 
 Node.js also supports syntax detection for ambiguous files. This feature applies to .js files or input strings where the module format is not explicitly defined. Node.js examines the source code and checks whether it contains syntax that cannot be executed as CommonJS. Examples include import statements, export statements, import.meta, top-level await, or lexical declarations that conflict with CommonJS wrapper variables such as require, module, or exports. If this syntax is detected, Node.js treats the source as an ES module.
 
 Although syntax detection provides flexibility, explicitly declaring the module type is recommended. Package authors should include a "type" field even when creating CommonJS packages. Being explicit avoids ambiguity, improves compatibility with development tools, and protects packages against possible future changes to Node.js defaults.
 
 The module system choice affects how files are resolved and loaded. CommonJS uses require(), while ES modules use static import statements or dynamic import(). These two systems follow different resolution rules, especially regarding file extensions, directory loading, and supported formats. Understanding how Node.js determines module types is essential for creating packages that behave consistently across different environments and versions.

title: Events
text:
Node.js uses an event-driven architecture where objects can emit named events and other parts of the application can listen and respond to those events. This system is based on the EventEmitter class, which is used throughout many Node.js core modules such as streams, servers, and file system operations.
 
 Error handling is an important part of working with EventEmitter. When an error occurs, Node.js emits a special event called error. Unlike normal events, an unhandled error event can cause the Node.js process to terminate. For this reason, applications should always register an error listener to properly manage failures and avoid unexpected crashes.
 
 Node.js also provides the errorMonitor feature, which allows developers to observe errors for logging or monitoring purposes without taking control of the error handling process. This is useful for diagnostic systems where errors need to be recorded while maintaining the default behavior.
 
 When using asynchronous functions as event listeners, rejected Promises can create unhandled errors. Node.js provides the captureRejections option to automatically redirect rejected Promises to the EventEmitter error system. This allows asynchronous errors to be handled using the same mechanism as regular event errors.
 
 The EventEmitter class is the foundation of Node.js event-based programming. It allows developers to create custom events, attach listener functions, and trigger events when specific actions occur. The on() method is used to register listeners, while the emit() method is used to execute all listeners connected to a particular event.
 
 Multiple listeners can be attached to the same event. When an event is emitted, the listeners are executed synchronously in the order they were registered. This predictable behavior allows developers to control the sequence of operations in asynchronous applications.
 
 The once() method allows developers to register a listener that executes only one time. After the event is triggered, the listener is automatically removed. This is useful for actions that should happen only during the first occurrence of an event, such as initialization tasks or first-time connections.
 
 Node.js also provides methods for removing listeners. The removeListener() and off() methods remove specific listener functions from an event, while removeAllListeners() removes all listeners associated with a particular event. These methods help manage application resources and prevent unnecessary event handlers from remaining active.
 
 EventEmitter includes a listener limit system to help detect possible memory leaks. By default, Node.js allows up to 10 listeners for a single event before displaying a warning. This limit does not prevent additional listeners from being added; instead, it alerts developers that an application may be creating too many event handlers. The limit can be adjusted with setMaxListeners() when necessary.
 
 Events are a fundamental concept in Node.js because they allow applications to efficiently handle asynchronous operations. Understanding EventEmitter, listeners, error handling, and event management is essential for building scalable applications with Node.js.

title: File system
text:
The node:fs module in Node.js provides an interface for interacting with the file system using methods based on standard POSIX functions. It allows developers to perform operations such as reading, writing, deleting, copying, modifying, and monitoring files and directories. The module can be accessed through different programming styles, including promise-based APIs with node:fs/promises, callback APIs with node:fs, and synchronous APIs. These approaches provide flexibility depending on the requirements of the application, especially regarding performance and control over asynchronous behavior.
 
 The promise-based API is commonly used in modern JavaScript because it works naturally with async and await. Methods such as readFile(), writeFile(), unlink(), and mkdir() return promises that are completed when the file system operation finishes. These operations run using Node.js’s internal thread pool, allowing file system tasks to execute outside the main event loop. However, these operations are not automatically synchronized, so developers must be careful when multiple operations modify the same file at the same time because data corruption may occur.
 
 The callback-based API performs operations asynchronously and executes a callback function after completion. The callback receives an error object as its first argument, which follows the common Node.js error-handling pattern. If the operation succeeds, the error argument is usually null or undefined. Although callbacks are older than promises, they can provide better performance in situations where maximum execution speed and reduced memory usage are important.
 
 The synchronous API is another option available in the fs module. Unlike asynchronous methods, synchronous functions block the Node.js event loop until the operation is completed. This means that JavaScript execution pauses while the file system task runs. Because of this behavior, synchronous methods are usually avoided in servers or applications that need high concurrency, but they can be useful in simple scripts, command-line tools, or initialization tasks where blocking execution is acceptable.
 
 The FileHandle class represents an opened file and provides more advanced control over file operations. A FileHandle object is created using fsPromises.open() and works as a wrapper around a file descriptor. Developers should always close file handles explicitly with close() to prevent resource leaks. File handles support many operations, including reading data, writing content, creating streams, changing permissions, synchronizing data with storage devices, and retrieving file information.
 
 Overall, the node:fs module is a fundamental part of Node.js development because it provides powerful tools for managing files efficiently. Understanding the differences between promise-based, callback, and synchronous APIs helps developers choose the most appropriate approach depending on application needs, performance requirements, and code maintainability.

title: Stream
text:
A stream is an abstract interface in Node.js designed for working with streaming data. Instead of loading all data into memory at once, streams allow applications to process data gradually as it becomes available. This approach is especially useful when handling large files, network communication, compression, encryption, or any situation where data arrives over time. The node:stream module provides the core API used to create and work with stream implementations.
 
 Many built-in Node.js objects are streams. For example, an HTTP request received by a server is a readable stream because data arrives from the client and can be consumed piece by piece. An HTTP response is a writable stream because the server writes data progressively back to the client. Other examples include process.stdout, file streams created with the fs module, TCP sockets, compression streams, and child process communication channels.
 
 Streams can have different capabilities depending on how they are designed. A Readable stream represents a source of data that an application can consume. A Writable stream represents a destination where data can be written. A Duplex stream supports both reading and writing independently, meaning it behaves as both a readable and writable stream. A Transform stream is a special type of Duplex stream that modifies or transforms data while it passes through the stream, such as compression or encryption operations.
 
 All streams in Node.js are instances of EventEmitter. This means they communicate state changes and data availability through events. For example, readable streams can emit events such as 'data', 'end', and 'error', while writable streams can emit events such as 'finish', 'drain', and 'close'. This event-based design allows applications to react asynchronously without blocking execution while waiting for data.
 
 The node:stream module is normally not required when simply consuming streams. Most applications use streams provided by Node.js APIs, such as fs.createReadStream() or HTTP request and response objects. The module becomes important when developers need to implement custom stream types or use advanced stream utilities.
 
 The module also provides helper functions that simplify stream management. stream.pipeline() connects multiple streams together and automatically handles errors and completion. stream.finished() allows code to wait until a stream has completely finished reading or writing. Readable.from() creates readable streams from iterables or asynchronous iterables, and stream.addAbortSignal() allows streams to be cancelled using an AbortSignal.
 
 The Streams Promises API, available through require('node:stream/promises'), provides promise-based versions of important utilities. Instead of relying on callbacks, these functions can be used with async and await, making stream-based code easier to organize and integrate with modern JavaScript asynchronous patterns.

title: Crear y probar en Node.js
text:
Crear un flujo de trabajo de integración continua (CI) en Node.js permite automatizar las tareas necesarias para verificar que un proyecto funciona correctamente después de cada cambio de código. Un flujo de trabajo de CI puede encargarse de construir la aplicación, instalar sus dependencias, ejecutar pruebas automatizadas y comprobar que las modificaciones realizadas no introducen errores. Cuando todas las pruebas de CI se completan correctamente, el mismo flujo puede ampliarse para realizar tareas adicionales como desplegar una aplicación o publicar un paquete.
 
 Para crear un flujo de trabajo de CI para un proyecto Node.js es recomendable tener conocimientos básicos de Node.js, YAML, la configuración de flujos de trabajo y la estructura de los archivos utilizados por Repositorio Actions. Los flujos de trabajo se definen mediante archivos YAML y normalmente se almacenan dentro del directorio .Repositorio/workflows del repositorio.
 
 Repositorio proporciona plantillas prediseñadas de flujos de trabajo para Node.js que permiten comenzar rápidamente. Estas plantillas incluyen una configuración inicial adecuada para la mayoría de los proyectos y pueden modificarse posteriormente según las necesidades específicas del equipo o de la aplicación. Para crear una plantilla, se debe acceder al repositorio en Repositorio, abrir la sección Actions, seleccionar la opción para crear un nuevo flujo de trabajo y buscar una plantilla relacionada con Node.js e integración continua.
 
 Después de seleccionar la plantilla de Node.js, Repositorio genera un archivo de configuración, normalmente con un nombre como node.js.yml, dentro del directorio .Repositorio/workflows. Este archivo define los pasos que ejecutará el sistema automáticamente. Los desarrolladores pueden modificarlo para cambiar las versiones de Node.js utilizadas, añadir comandos personalizados, configurar variables de entorno o incorporar procesos adicionales.
 
 Una parte fundamental de cualquier flujo de trabajo de Node.js es definir qué versión del entorno debe utilizarse. La forma recomendada de hacerlo en Repositorio Actions es mediante la acción setup-node. Esta acción recibe una versión específica de Node.js como entrada y la configura dentro del ejecutor donde se ejecuta el flujo de trabajo.
 
 La acción setup-node busca la versión solicitada dentro de la caché de herramientas disponible en el ejecutor y agrega los archivos binarios necesarios al PATH del sistema. Esto permite que todos los pasos posteriores del flujo puedan utilizar esa versión de Node.js de manera consistente. Esta práctica es importante porque garantiza que las pruebas y compilaciones produzcan resultados similares independientemente del ejecutor utilizado.
 
 Cuando se utilizan ejecutores administrados por Repositorio, la acción setup-node simplifica la configuración del entorno. Sin embargo, si se utiliza un ejecutor autohospedado, el administrador debe instalar Node.js manualmente y asegurarse de que esté correctamente añadido al PATH.

title: Numpy: trabajando computación cientifica con Python
text:
Introducción
 En aplicaciones científicas, de ingeniería y principalmente de ciencia de datos, existe la necesidad de realizar cálculos numéricos especializados.
 Cuando haces la suma de todos los valores de una columna en un software de hojas de cálculo o incluso operaciones matemáticas entre diferentes columnas, hay un código implementado para hacer estas operaciones posibles. De la misma manera, si has utilizado una función de una biblioteca de Python que realiza regresión lineal o un algoritmo de machine learning cualquiera, debes saber que este código es la traducción de un conjunto de ecuaciones matemáticas a código. Esta implementación necesita ser eficiente y fácil de comprender. Cuanto más cercano esté el código escrito a la escritura matemática, mejor.
 En este contexto, en Python, surge NumPy. Esta es una poderosa biblioteca ampliamente utilizada que ha revolucionado el segmento de computación científica, principalmente debido al carácter abierto del lenguaje Python. Con NumPy, es posible realizar operaciones matemáticas complejas con matrices de forma eficiente y optimizada. ¿Pero qué es exactamente y cómo funciona NumPy?
 ¿Qué es NumPy?
 NumPy, una abreviatura de Numerical Python, es una biblioteca de código abierto de Python para computación científica, un campo de estudio que utiliza recursos computacionales para comprender y resolver problemas. Esta biblioteca permite trabajar con la manipulación de objetos array multidimensionales, así como con sus derivados, como matrices, secuencias y otros. Además de eso, también posee una amplia variedad de operaciones rápidas con los arrays, incluyendo operaciones matemáticas y lógicas, manipulación de formato, ordenación y selección, herramientas de estadística y cálculo, y mucho más.
 La biblioteca NumPy fue lanzada en 2005 por el científico de datos Travis Oliphant, con la propuesta de ser una herramienta rápida, eficiente y fácil de usar, permitiendo así la realización de cálculos numéricos y matemáticos a gran escala, a través de la funcionalidad llamada vectorización. Por eso, se ha convertido en una de las bases fundamentales para el análisis de datos, el aprendizaje automático (machine learning) y la computación científica en general, estando presente también en la construcción de varias bibliotecas de ciencia de datos, incluyendo: Pandas, Matplotlib, Scikit-learn, SciPy, y mucho más.
 Una curiosidad sobre esta biblioteca es que también ha estado presente en trabajos de descubrimientos científicos importantes, como la detección de la primera imagen de un agujero negro y la detección de ondas gravitacionales.
 ¿Pero cómo funciona exactamente NumPy?
 Estructuras básicas de NumPy
 NumPy funciona a través de estructuras llamadas arrays, que son estructuras de datos homogéneas, es decir, donde los elementos poseen el mismo tipo. Estas estructuras pueden tener varios formatos y dimensiones, que varían según las necesidades de cada tipo de proyecto. De manera general, para varios tipos de aplicación, trabajamos hasta la tercera dimensión, pero existen casos donde podemos necesitar más.

title: CSS
text:
Hojas de Estilo en Cascada (del inglés Cascading Style Sheets) o CSS es el lenguaje de estilos utilizado para describir la presentación de documentos HTML o XML (incluyendo varios lenguajes basados en XML como SVG, MathML o XHTML). CSS describe cómo debe ser renderizado el elemento estructurado en la pantalla, en papel, en el habla o en otros medios.

CSS es uno de los lenguajes base de la Open Web y posee una especificación estandarizada por parte del W3C. Anteriormente , el desarrollo de varias partes de las especificaciones de CSS era realizado de manera sincrónica, lo que permitía el versionado de las recomendaciones. Probablemente habrás escuchado acerca de CSS1, CSS2.1, CSS3. Sin embargo, CSS4 nunca se ha lanzado como una versión oficial.

Desde CSS3, el alcance de las especificaciones se incrementó de forma significativa y el progreso de los diferentes módulos de CSS comenzó a mostrar varias diferencias, lo que hizo más efectivo desarrollar y publicar recomendaciones separadas por módulos. title: DOM Manipulation
text:
In the 20+ years since its standardization, JavaScript has come a very long way. While in 2020, JavaScript can be used on servers, in data science, and even on IoT devices, it is important to remember its most popular use case: web browsers.

Websites are made up of HTML and/or XML documents. These documents are static, they do not change. The Document Object Model (DOM) is a programming interface implemented by browsers to make static websites functional. The DOM API can be used to change the document structure, style, and content. The API is so powerful that countless frontend frameworks (jQuery, React, Angular, etc.) have been developed around it to make dynamic websites even easier to develop.

TypeScript is a typed superset of JavaScript, and it ships type definitions for the DOM API. These definitions are readily available in any default TypeScript project. Of the 20,000+ lines of definitions in lib.dom.d.ts, one stands out among the rest: HTMLElement. This type is the backbone for DOM manipulation with TypeScript.
